title: Your own body
hookLine: several traditions honor the body as gift or temple

lines: KNEES THAT CLICK ON THE STAIRS.
WORDS SAID SILENTLY TO A BODY.
cards: Knees that click on the stairs. A back that votes against getting out of bed. A face under the bathroom light at seven in the morning.
For some people, the harshest words of the whole day are said silently, to their own body.

Meanwhile that same body has been breathing all night without being asked, healing a paper cut nobody thanked it for, and carrying its owner to the mirror to be criticized. This stretch of the path is about love.
Today it turns to the one thing every listener is living in.

teach.b: First, fearfully and wonderfully made. In the Psalms, a singer looks at their own body and starts praising: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Not perfectly made, not admired by others.
Wonderfully, with a little awe mixed in. The body is a gift and a wonder before it's anything else.

Second, a temple, not a project. Writing to Christians in Corinth who were arguing about what they could do with their bodies, Paul asks: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you".
In context he's warning them about how they use their bodies, and the image raises the stakes: a temple is holy, a place where God dwells, not something to use carelessly.

Third, the Buddha accepts a meal. In a sutta in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha remembers his life before awakening. He tried to wring freedom out of his body by starving it, until it was skin and bone.
It didn't work. Then he remembered sitting peacefully under a tree as a boy, and asked whether that kind of ease was really something to fear. He decided it wasn't, and took solid food again.
The way forward began with a meal.
Fourth, kind, not perfect. None of these texts asks for a body that looks a certain way. They ask for something smaller: reverence, care, an end to treating it as an enemy.
Sleep when it's tired. Feed it.

how: Some Christians speak of the body as a temple, after Paul's letter to the Corinthians; Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including the praise of being wonderfully made; Buddhists tell how the Buddha left behind extreme fasting and took food before his awakening.

o: a body that must be kept perfect to be holy
a building where people go to worship on weekends
Paul's word for the body: holy, a place where God dwells

games.q: who said what about the body — tap the pairs.
p: left starving behind and ate again
holy, not something to use carelessly

it says fearfully and wonderfully made.

it didn't work; he took solid food again.

1 Corinthians, written to a church arguing about the body.

games.q: you're the young seeker. a long stretch of starving has left you skin and bone, and no closer to freedom. what do you do?
o: fast harder; it must be working.
eat a real meal and keep going.
give up the search for good.
games.why: in the sutta, he remembers a peaceful moment from boyhood, decides ease isn't to be feared, and takes solid food again.

practice: Sit or lie down, whatever is kind to your back, and move your attention slowly from the feet upward, legs, belly, hands, shoulders, face, silently thanking each part for today.

Wherever there's an ache, rest there for a breath the way you'd sit with a tired friend, and if the old critical words show up, let them pass and go back to thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this body.

wordCard.voice: Temple. Paul's word for the body: a place where God dwells, to be cared for, not used carelessly. Today's word.

orig.note: the Greek word for temple that Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 6:19.

carryVoice: Your line: this body. It has been carrying you all along. That's day eight hundred fifty-nine.
